--- title: "Hands-on_Ex06b" format: html: toc: true toc-depth: 3 number-sections: true code-fold: false editor: visual execute: freeze: auto --- # Visual Correlation Analysis ## Overview Correlation analysis is used to examine how two numerical variables move together. A correlation coefficient ranges from -1 to 1. A value close to 1 means a strong positive linear relationship, a value close to -1 means a strong negative linear relationship, and a value close to 0 means there is no clear linear relationship. When a dataset contains many numerical variables, checking every pair one by one is inefficient. A correlation matrix helps us compare all pairwise relationships in one structured view. A corrgram then turns this matrix into a visual display, making strong, weak, positive and negative relationships easier to detect. In this hands-on exercise, we use the wine quality dataset to explore different methods for visualising correlation: - scatterplot matrix using `pairs()`; - correlation matrix using `ggstatsplot`; - separate correlation matrices for red and white wine; - corrgram using `corrplot`; - mixed corrgram with both shapes and numbers; - significance testing for correlation pairs; - reordered corrgram to reveal hidden structure. ## Installing and Launching R Packages The main packages used in this exercise are: - `tidyverse` for data import and wrangling; - `corrplot` for correlation matrix visualisation; - `ggstatsplot` for statistical correlation plots; - `knitr` for displaying tables. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pacman::p_load(corrplot, ggstatsplot, tidyverse, knitr) ``` ::: ## Importing and Preparing The Data Set In this exercise, the wine quality dataset is used. The dataset contains physicochemical attributes of wine, such as acidity, sugar, chlorides, sulphur dioxide, density, pH, sulphates and alcohol. It also includes wine quality score and wine type. The key idea is to study how these numerical wine attributes are correlated with each other. ### Importing Data To avoid path problems during rendering, the code below checks several possible locations for `wine_quality.csv`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} wine_path <- case_when( file.exists("wine_quality.csv") ~ "wine_quality.csv", file.exists("data/wine_quality.csv") ~ "data/wine_quality.csv", file.exists("../data/wine_quality.csv") ~ "../data/wine_quality.csv", file.exists("../../data/wine_quality.csv") ~ "../../data/wine_quality.csv", TRUE ~ NA_character_ ) if (is.na(wine_path)) { stop("wine_quality.csv cannot be found. Please place it in this folder or in the data folder.") } wine <- read_csv(wine_path) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Rows: 6497 Columns: 13 ── Column specification ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Delimiter: "," chr (1): type dbl (12): fixed acidity, volatile acidity, citric acid, residual sugar, chlo... ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data. ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message. ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} glimpse(wine) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rows: 6,497 Columns: 13 $ `fixed acidity` 7.4, 7.8, 7.8, 11.2, 7.4, 7.4, 7.9, 7.3, 7.8, 7… $ `volatile acidity` 0.700, 0.880, 0.760, 0.280, 0.700, 0.660, 0.600… $ `citric acid` 0.00, 0.00, 0.04, 0.56, 0.00, 0.00, 0.06, 0.00,… $ `residual sugar` 1.9, 2.6, 2.3, 1.9, 1.9, 1.8, 1.6, 1.2, 2.0, 6.… $ chlorides 0.076, 0.098, 0.092, 0.075, 0.076, 0.075, 0.069… $ `free sulfur dioxide` 11, 25, 15, 17, 11, 13, 15, 15, 9, 17, 15, 17, … $ `total sulfur dioxide` 34, 67, 54, 60, 34, 40, 59, 21, 18, 102, 65, 10… $ density 0.9978, 0.9968, 0.9970, 0.9980, 0.9978, 0.9978,… $ pH 3.51, 3.20, 3.26, 3.16, 3.51, 3.51, 3.30, 3.39,… $ sulphates 0.56, 0.68, 0.65, 0.58, 0.56, 0.56, 0.46, 0.47,… $ alcohol 9.4, 9.8, 9.8, 9.8, 9.4, 9.4, 9.4, 10.0, 9.5, 1… $ quality 5, 5, 5, 6, 5, 5, 5, 7, 7, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5,… $ type "red", "red", "red", "red", "red", "red", "red"… ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} knitr::kable(head(wine), format = "html") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

The wine `type` variable is useful for grouping, but it should not be placed directly inside a numerical correlation matrix. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} wine_num <- wine %>% select(where(is.numeric)) glimpse(wine_num) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rows: 6,497 Columns: 12 $ `fixed acidity` 7.4, 7.8, 7.8, 11.2, 7.4, 7.4, 7.9, 7.3, 7.8, 7… $ `volatile acidity` 0.700, 0.880, 0.760, 0.280, 0.700, 0.660, 0.600… $ `citric acid` 0.00, 0.00, 0.04, 0.56, 0.00, 0.00, 0.06, 0.00,… $ `residual sugar` 1.9, 2.6, 2.3, 1.9, 1.9, 1.8, 1.6, 1.2, 2.0, 6.… $ chlorides 0.076, 0.098, 0.092, 0.075, 0.076, 0.075, 0.069… $ `free sulfur dioxide` 11, 25, 15, 17, 11, 13, 15, 15, 9, 17, 15, 17, … $ `total sulfur dioxide` 34, 67, 54, 60, 34, 40, 59, 21, 18, 102, 65, 10… $ density 0.9978, 0.9968, 0.9970, 0.9980, 0.9978, 0.9978,… $ pH 3.51, 3.20, 3.26, 3.16, 3.51, 3.51, 3.30, 3.39,… $ sulphates 0.56, 0.68, 0.65, 0.58, 0.56, 0.56, 0.46, 0.47,… $ alcohol 9.4, 9.8, 9.8, 9.8, 9.4, 9.4, 9.4, 10.0, 9.5, 1… $ quality 5, 5, 5, 6, 5, 5, 5, 7, 7, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5,… ``` ::: ::: ## Building Correlation Matrix: pairs() method The base R function `pairs()` creates a scatterplot matrix. It is a quick way to inspect pairwise relationships among several numerical variables. The advantage of `pairs()` is that it is simple and does not require much setup. The limitation is that the plot can become crowded when there are many variables or many observations. ### Building a basic correlation matrix The first plot uses the default `pairs()` function on the numerical wine variables. ::: {.panel-tabset} ## The plot ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pairs(wine_num) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Hands-on_Ex06b_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## The code chunk ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pairs(wine_num) ``` ::: ::: This scatterplot matrix gives a quick overview of pairwise relationships. However, because the wine dataset has many observations, the panels can look dense and difficult to interpret. ### Drawing the lower corner A correlation matrix is symmetric. The upper triangle and lower triangle contain the same variable pairs. Therefore, it is often cleaner to display only one side of the matrix. ::: {.panel-tabset} ## The plot ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pairs(wine_num, upper.panel = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Hands-on_Ex06b_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## The code chunk ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pairs(wine_num, upper.panel = NULL) ``` ::: ::: This version reduces visual duplication. It keeps the lower scatterplot panels and removes the repeated upper half. We can also remove the lower panels and display only the upper half. ::: {.panel-tabset} ## The plot ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pairs(wine_num, lower.panel = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Hands-on_Ex06b_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## The code chunk ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pairs(wine_num, lower.panel = NULL) ``` ::: ::: The choice between upper and lower panel is mainly a design choice. The analytical content is the same. ### Including with correlation coefficients Instead of showing scatterplots in every panel, we can display correlation coefficients in one part of the matrix. The custom function below prints the absolute correlation coefficient and enlarges the number when the relationship is stronger. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} panel.cor <- function(x, y, digits = 2, prefix = "", cex.cor, ...) { usr <- par("usr") on.exit(par(usr)) par(usr = c(0, 1, 0, 1)) r <- abs(cor(x, y, use = "complete.obs")) txt <- format(c(r, 0.123456789), digits = digits)[1] txt <- paste(prefix, txt, sep = "") if (missing(cex.cor)) cex.cor <- 0.8 / strwidth(txt) text(0.5, 0.5, txt, cex = cex.cor * (1 + r) / 2) } ``` ::: ::: {.panel-tabset} ## The plot ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pairs(wine_num, upper.panel = panel.cor) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning in par(usr): argument 1 does not name a graphical parameter Warning in par(usr): argument 1 r) / 2) } pairs(wine_num, upper.panel = panel.cor) ``` ::: ::: This design is more informative than the default scatterplot matrix because it combines shape inspection with numerical correlation strength. ## Visualising Correlation Matrix: ggcorrmat() When the dataset is large, scatterplot matrices can become too crowded. A corrgram is often more useful because it compresses the relationships into a clean matrix. In this section, `ggstatsplot::ggcorrmat()` is used. It creates a correlation matrix and includes statistical reporting directly in the visual output. ### The basic plot ::: {.panel-tabset} ## The plot ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggstatsplot::ggcorrmat( data = wine_num ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Hands-on_Ex06b_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## The code chunk ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggstatsplot::ggcorrmat( data = wine_num ) ``` ::: ::: This chart shows the pairwise correlations among the selected wine variables. It is easier to read than the scatterplot matrix when the main goal is to compare correlation strength. The next version customises the plot with hierarchical ordering, black outlines and a clearer title. ::: {.panel-tabset} ## The plot ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggstatsplot::ggcorrmat( data = wine_num, ggcorrplot.args = list( outline.color = "black", hc.order = TRUE, tl.cex = 10, colors = c("#D95F02", "white", "#2A6F6F") ), title = "Correlogram for Wine Quality Dataset", subtitle = "Correlation matrix with hierarchical ordering" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` integer(0) ``` ::: ::: ## The code chunk ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggstatsplot::ggcorrmat( data = wine_num, ggcorrplot.args = list( outline.color = "black", hc.order = TRUE, tl.cex = 10, colors = c("#D95F02", "white", "#2A6F6F") ), title = "Correlogram for Wine Quality Dataset", subtitle = "Correlation matrix with hierarchical ordering" ) ``` ::: ::: The hierarchical ordering helps place similar variables closer together. This makes clusters of related variables easier to detect. ## Building multiple plots The original idea is to compare the correlation structure across red wine and white wine. Instead of using `grouped_ggcorrmat()`, which may fail during Quarto rendering, this version creates two separate correlation matrices. This is more stable and easier to display on the website. ### Red wine correlation matrix ::: {.panel-tabset} ## The plot ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} wine_red <- wine %>% filter(type == "red") %>% select(where(is.numeric)) ggstatsplot::ggcorrmat( data = wine_red, ggcorrplot.args = list( outline.color = "black", hc.order = TRUE, tl.cex = 9, colors = c("#D95F02", "white", "#2A6F6F") ), title = "Correlogram for Red Wine", subtitle = "Correlation matrix for red wine observations only" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` integer(0) ``` ::: ::: ## The code chunk ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} wine_red <- wine %>% filter(type == "red") %>% select(where(is.numeric)) ggstatsplot::ggcorrmat( data = wine_red, ggcorrplot.args = list( outline.color = "black", hc.order = TRUE, tl.cex = 9, colors = c("#D95F02", "white", "#2A6F6F") ), title = "Correlogram for Red Wine", subtitle = "Correlation matrix for red wine observations only" ) ``` ::: ::: ### White wine correlation matrix ::: {.panel-tabset} ## The plot ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} wine_white <- wine %>% filter(type == "white") %>% select(where(is.numeric)) ggstatsplot::ggcorrmat( data = wine_white, ggcorrplot.args = list( outline.color = "black", hc.order = TRUE, tl.cex = 9, colors = c("#D95F02", "white", "#2A6F6F") ), title = "Correlogram for White Wine", subtitle = "Correlation matrix for white wine observations only" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` integer(0) ``` ::: ::: ## The code chunk ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} wine_white <- wine %>% filter(type == "white") %>% select(where(is.numeric)) ggstatsplot::ggcorrmat( data = wine_white, ggcorrplot.args = list( outline.color = "black", hc.order = TRUE, tl.cex = 9, colors = c("#D95F02", "white", "#2A6F6F") ), title = "Correlogram for White Wine", subtitle = "Correlation matrix for white wine observations only" ) ``` ::: ::: This grouped comparison is more analytical than one overall matrix. It shows whether the same chemical attributes behave similarly across wine types or whether the correlation structure changes. ## Visualising Correlation Matrix using corrplot Package The `corrplot` package is one of the most commonly used tools for visualising correlation matrices in R. It provides several visual forms such as circles, ellipses, numbers, shades, colours and pies. Before plotting, we first compute the correlation matrix using `cor()`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} wine.cor <- cor(wine_num, use = "complete.obs") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} round(wine.cor[1:5, 1:5], 2) %>% knitr::kable(format = "html") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
fixed acidity volatile acidity citric acid residual sugar chlorides
fixed acidity 1.00 0.22 0.32 -0.11 0.30
volatile acidity 0.22 1.00 -0.38 -0.20 0.38
citric acid 0.32 -0.38 1.00 0.14 0.04
residual sugar -0.11 -0.20 0.14 1.00 -0.13
chlorides 0.30 0.38 0.04 -0.13 1.00
````` ::: ::: ### Getting started with corrplot The simplest `corrplot()` call uses the default circle method and full matrix layout. ::: {.panel-tabset} ## The plot ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} corrplot(wine.cor) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Hands-on_Ex06b_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-25-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## The code chunk ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} corrplot(wine.cor) ``` ::: ::: The default corrplot uses colour and circle size to show correlation direction and strength. Strong positive correlations and strong negative correlations are visually more intense. ### Working with visual geometrics The `method` argument controls how correlations are represented. Here, the ellipse method is used. A thin ellipse indicates a stronger relationship, while a rounder ellipse indicates a weaker relationship. ::: {.panel-tabset} ## The plot ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} corrplot(wine.cor, method = "ellipse") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Hands-on_Ex06b_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-27-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## The code chunk ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} corrplot(wine.cor, method = "ellipse") ``` ::: ::: The ellipse method is useful because it visually encodes both direction and magnitude in a compact way. ### Working with layout The `type` argument controls whether the full, lower or upper matrix is displayed. Since the matrix is symmetric, showing only the lower part is usually enough. ::: {.panel-tabset} ## The plot ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} corrplot(wine.cor, method = "ellipse", type = "lower") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Hands-on_Ex06b_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-29-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## The code chunk ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} corrplot(wine.cor, method = "ellipse", type = "lower") ``` ::: ::: The next version removes the diagonal and changes the text labels to black. This makes the corrgram cleaner for presentation. ::: {.panel-tabset} ## The plot ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} corrplot(wine.cor, method = "ellipse", type = "lower", diag = FALSE, tl.col = "black") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Hands-on_Ex06b_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-31-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## The code chunk ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} corrplot(wine.cor, method = "ellipse", type = "lower", diag = FALSE, tl.col = "black") ``` ::: ::: This version is easier to read because it removes unnecessary self-correlations on the diagonal. ### Working with mixed layout A mixed corrgram can show shapes in one triangle and numbers in the other triangle. This gives both visual and numerical interpretation in one chart. ::: {.panel-tabset} ## The plot ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} corrplot.mixed( wine.cor, lower = "ellipse", upper = "number", tl.pos = "lt", diag = "l", tl.col = "black" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Hands-on_Ex06b_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-33-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## The code chunk ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} corrplot.mixed( wine.cor, lower = "ellipse", upper = "number", tl.pos = "lt", diag = "l", tl.col = "black" ) ``` ::: ::: This layout is efficient. The lower half gives the visual pattern, while the upper half gives the exact correlation coefficients. ### Combining corrgram with the significant test A correlation coefficient may look large or small, but we should also check whether it is statistically significant. The function below computes p-values and confidence intervals for each pair of variables. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cor.mtest <- function(mat, conf.level = 0.95) { mat <- as.matrix(mat) n <- ncol(mat) p.mat <- lowCI.mat <- uppCI.mat <- matrix(NA, n, n) diag(p.mat) <- 0 diag(lowCI.mat) <- diag(uppCI.mat) <- 1 for (i in 1:(n - 1)) { for (j in (i + 1):n) { tmp <- cor.test(mat[, i], mat[, j], conf.level = conf.level) p.mat[i, j] <- p.mat[j, i] <- tmp$p.value lowCI.mat[i, j] <- lowCI.mat[j, i] <- tmp$conf.int[1] uppCI.mat[i, j] <- uppCI.mat[j, i] <- tmp$conf.int[2] } } colnames(p.mat) <- rownames(p.mat) <- colnames(mat) colnames(lowCI.mat) <- rownames(lowCI.mat) <- colnames(mat) colnames(uppCI.mat) <- rownames(uppCI.mat) <- colnames(mat) return(list(p = p.mat, lowCI = lowCI.mat, uppCI = uppCI.mat)) } ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} wine.sig <- cor.mtest(wine_num, conf.level = 0.95) ``` ::: ::: {.panel-tabset} ## The plot ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} corrplot( wine.cor, method = "number", type = "lower", diag = FALSE, tl.col = "black", tl.srt = 45, p.mat = wine.sig$p, sig.level = 0.05 ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Hands-on_Ex06b_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-37-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## The code chunk ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} wine.sig <- cor.mtest(wine_num, conf.level = 0.95) corrplot( wine.cor, method = "number", type = "lower", diag = FALSE, tl.col = "black", tl.srt = 45, p.mat = wine.sig$p, sig.level = 0.05 ) ``` ::: ::: This plot is useful because it prevents us from reading every numerical correlation as equally meaningful. Non-significant pairs are visually marked, so the interpretation becomes more cautious. ### Reorder a corrgram Reordering variables can reveal hidden structure in the matrix. Without reordering, the variables follow the original dataset order. With reordering, highly related variables are placed closer together. ::: {.panel-tabset} ## The plot ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} corrplot.mixed( wine.cor, lower = "ellipse", upper = "number", tl.pos = "lt", diag = "l", order = "AOE", tl.col = "black" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Hands-on_Ex06b_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-39-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## The code chunk ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} corrplot.mixed( wine.cor, lower = "ellipse", upper = "number", tl.pos = "lt", diag = "l", order = "AOE", tl.col = "black" ) ``` ::: ::: The `AOE` order is based on angular order of eigenvectors. In practical terms, it tries to place variables with similar correlation patterns closer together. We can also use hierarchical clustering. ::: {.panel-tabset} ## The plot ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} corrplot( wine.cor, method = "ellipse", type = "lower", order = "hclust", hclust.method = "ward.D2", diag = FALSE, tl.col = "black", col = colorRampPalette(c("#D95F02", "white", "#2A6F6F"))(200) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Hands-on_Ex06b_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-41-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## The code chunk ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} corrplot( wine.cor, method = "ellipse", type = "lower", order = "hclust", hclust.method = "ward.D2", diag = FALSE, tl.col = "black", col = colorRampPalette(c("#D95F02", "white", "#2A6F6F"))(200) ) ``` ::: ::: This reordered corrgram is useful when we want to discover groups of variables that behave similarly. ## My Extension: Correlation with Wine Quality As a small extension, we can focus specifically on the relationship between wine quality and the other numerical attributes.
